title: CVE-2024-7264: ASN.1 date parser overread
excerpt:
## Summary:

When a specially-crafted certificate is passed to `Curl_extract_certinfo` to parse, it may read bytes beyond the end of the buffer in which the certificate is held. According to the application, this may be a stack read overflow or a heap read overflow.

Specifically the issue is in function `GTime2str`, in which the specially-crafted input may cause it to set `fracl = -1` and then pass it to `Curl_dyn_addf`, which in turn treats this `-1` as "no length given" and goes on to run `strlen(tzp)` which goes beyond the end of the certificate buffer (assuming there are no null bytes).

I believe the issue is in this loop (in `lib/vtls/x509asn1.c`):

```
 524     /* Strip leading zeroes in fractional seconds. */
 525     for(fracl = tzp - fracp - 1; fracl && fracp[fracl - 1] == '0'; fracl--)
 526       ;
```

If `tzp == fracp`, then `fracl` is set to -1 in the loop initialization.

I tested this on curl 8.9.0 commit `2a59c8d4cebfd199f930213ee82ae95f71e44578` (2024-07-24). I haven't looked when the issue was introduced.

## Steps To Reproduce:

  1. Compile libcurl with `-fsanitize=address` and with gnutls. I used clang. `CC=clang CFLAGS=-fsanitize=address ../configure --disable-shared --enable-debug --with-gnutls=/usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu`
  1. Compile the attached `poc.c` program which uses libcurl's `Curl_extract_certinfo`.
  1. Run `./poc bad_cert_1.bin` 

The resulting report from AddressSanitizer:

summary: A specially-crafted certificate causes a stack-buffer-overflow in curl's ASN.1 date parser when using gnutls, leading to out-of-bounds reads during certificate parsing.

claims.text: The loop in GTime2str may set fracl to -1 when tzp == fracp, causing Curl_dyn_addf to treat it as 'no length given' and run strlen(tzp) beyond the buffer
claims.reasoning: When a certificate ends with '.' or ',' (fractional indicator) and no digits follow, tzp==fracp at line 525, making fracl = SIZE_MAX. Cast to int for %.*s gives -1, which formatf treats as 'no precision' and calls strlen(fracp). Since fracp==end (just past the certificate buffer), strlen reads out of bounds. The loop at line 525 also reads fracp[SIZE_MAX-1], but the observed crash is in strlen from the format call.

claims.reasoning: A certificate where the fractional indicator ('.' or ',') is the last byte causes fracp to advance to end, tzp to advance to end (one increment), making tzp==fracp==end at line 525, so fracl = SIZE_MAX.

claims.text: The out-of-bounds strlen(tzp) read overflows the certificate buffer, causing a stack-buffer-overflow
claims.reasoning: The crash is in strlen(fracp) (not strlen(tzp) as the report states) when %.*s receives -1 precision. The AddressSanitizer stack trace confirms strlen reading 4471 bytes starting just past the stack buffer (offset 8224), matching fracp==end.

key_reasons: The code confirms a real buffer over-read in GTime2str when a certificate ends with a fractional indicator ('.' or ',') and no digits: fracl becomes SIZE_MAX, casts to -1 for %.*s, causing strlen(fracp) to read past the buffer.

However, curl's documented policy explicitly states: 'If a malicious server can trigger a NULL dereference in curl or otherwise cause curl to crash (and nothing worse), chances are big that we do not consider that a security problem.' This is a crash (DoS) from a malicious server certificate with no demonstrated data leak or code execution.
The report itself notes: 'I couldn't see a way where the remote attacker can actually get the content of the over-read memory bytes.'
reply: Thank you for the detailed report and reproduction case. The code confirms the buffer over-read in GTime2str when a certificate ends with '.' or ',' and no fractional digits: fracl wraps to SIZE_MAX, casts to -1 for the %.*s format, and strlen reads past the buffer. However, per curl's vulnerability disclosure policy (section 'NULL dereferences and crashes'), a crash triggered by a malicious server certificate—without data leakage or code execution—is not treated as a security vulnerability. We would still fix the bug as a robustness issue, but it does not qualify for a CVE or security advisory. If you can demonstrate a path to information disclosure or code execution, please share those details.
